title: Centre weighs special session to retry delimitation and women’s quota bill; Congress calls it bluff
dek: The constitutional amendment to enlarge the Lok Sabha fell short of a two-thirds majority in April. The government now says it has the numbers, according to reports.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Union government is considering calling a special session of Parliament to pass a constitutional amendment that would enlarge the Lok Sabha through delimitation and bring in 33% reservation for women, seven months after a similar bill failed to win the two-thirds majority it needed, according to reports. The Congress has dismissed the plan as bluff.

No dates have been announced. According to reports citing unnamed government sources, the government believes it now has 15 to 18 votes more than it needs. A constitutional amendment needs a two-thirds majority of members present and voting; with a full turnout, that means 361 votes in the 543-member House, which currently has three vacancies, according to reports.

## What the government wants to pass

The package taken up in the Lok Sabha in April, introduced on 16 April by Arjun Ram Meghwal, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Law and Justice, included the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, and the Delimitation Bill, 2026. They would raise the number of Lok Sabha seats from 543 to as many as 850, with 815 from the states and 35 from Union territories, and let a Delimitation Commission start work before the 2027 Census is complete. The aim is to bring in reserved seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies before the 2029 general election.

On 17 April, at a special sitting during the Budget Session, the constitutional amendment fell short of a two-thirds majority. During that debate Home Minister Amit Shah told the House that the southern states' seats would rise from 129 to 195, and their share of the total from 23.76% to 23.87%.

Reports say the government is now looking at raising every state's seats by 50% while keeping the shares between states as they are, to meet the southern states' objection that population-based redrawing would cut their weight in Parliament. Reports differ on which census those shares would be based on, and say no final decision has been taken.

## The Congress response

Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said on Thursday that Mr Shah had told a group of journalists informally that afternoon that "a 3-day special session will soon be called and the Bills will be passed by a 15-18 vote margin".

"He had said the same thing seven months earlier," Mr Ramesh wrote on X, saying the bill had then fallen short "by over 50 votes". "He is the master of bluff and bluster. His bulldozer did not work then and will not work again," he wrote. The government and the BJP have not responded publicly to his remarks, and Mr Shah has not commented on the record.

The INDIA bloc of opposition parties wants 33% reservation for women brought in at once within the current 543 seats, and opposes tying it to delimitation.

## A session that has not ended

The plan is possible partly because Parliament has never formally closed its last session. The Monsoon Session began on 20 July and both Houses were adjourned sine die on 13 August, but the President has not prorogued them. At 91 days, according to reports, that is the longest such gap on record, passing 87 days in 2008. The Constitution sets no deadline for prorogation.

The difference matters for timing. Reconvening the existing session needs at least two days' notice, according to reports, while a fresh session needs at least 14.

## Why it matters

Delimitation decides how many MPs each state sends to Parliament for decades. Southern states such as Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, which slowed their population growth earlier, have argued that redrawing seats by population would shift power to the north. West Bengal, with 42 Lok Sabha seats, would also see its number change under any new formula.

## What happens next

The government has not set a date. A special session could be called at short notice. The Winter Session of Parliament usually begins in late November or early December.
